大鑼屬體鳴樂器，基本發聲方式是以槌敲擊金屬鑼面。懸掛式大鑼通常以繩穿過近上緣孔洞: The tam-tam is an idiophone: the basic way of sounding it is to strike the metal face with a beater. A hanging tam-tam is usually hung vertically on a rope through holes near the top edge and then struck with a beater or a smaller drumstick; a bossed gong is mostly hung horizontally, and the central boss or the area beside it can be struck for different notes. On a large flat gong a light stroke can be made before the main stroke so that the sound arrives sooner, but a beginner must practise so that the light stroke is not heard. Smaller hanging gongs can be struck with bamboo sticks or Western drumsticks, and modern music also uses friction mallets, double bass bows or wooden, plastic and metal strikers.
大鑼屬體鳴樂器，霍恩博斯特尔—薩克斯編號111.241，常見於東南亞與東亞音樂傳: The tam-tam is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.241, common in the musical traditions of Southeast and East Asia. It can be struck on its own to give a crash, or used in tuned sets to give bell-like notes; it appears in Indonesian gamelan, the Philippine kulintang, Chinese opera, Japanese Buddhist ritual, kabuki and Japanese traditional accompaniment, and has also entered the percussion section of the Western symphony orchestra. Examples include Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring, symphonies by Mahler, Tchaikovsky and Shostakovich, and Stockhausen's Momente.
大鑼音色深沉而富有穿透力，具有獨特的暗沉質感，帶著青銅材質特有的溫潤韻味。其音域: The tam-tam's timbre is deep and strongly carrying, with a dark quality of its own and the warmth particular to bronze. Its range is wide, from a dull low boom to a clear bright crash in the middle and upper frequencies, and its timbre is rich in layers. After the stroke, the sound waves resonate complexly in the metal disc and the sound dies away gradually, spreading like ripples. Compared with the bright sharpness of a brass gong, the tam-tam is more restrained; compared with bells, it sounds more primitive and rough. Its resonance is distinctive and can create a mysterious, ethereal atmosphere, and it is often used to set off solemn or bleak moods.

The tam-tam is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.241, a kind of gong. It is usually a metal disc, flat, slightly concave or bowl-shaped, in various sizes, and is usually struck with a beater; it can give a crash on its own, or be tuned in sets to give bell-like notes. It is widely used in the musical traditions of Southeast and East Asia, and also appears in the percussion section of the Western symphony orchestra, in Chinese opera accompaniment, in temple ritual, in gamelan, and in Japanese Buddhist services, kabuki and ship-departure signals.
The tam-tam is an idiophone, Hornbostel–Sachs number 111.241. Its earliest possible image is on the surface of the Ngoc Lu bronze drum of the Dong Son culture in northern Vietnam (about the third to second century BC), which shows a seven-gong ensemble. In the sixth century AD Chinese texts describe it as a foreign instrument from between Tibet and Burma; the word gong comes from Java in Indonesia. Archaeology and scientific study indicate that Annam, Java, Burma and southern China were manufacturing centres of the ancient world. It reached the West in the eighteenth century and entered the percussion section of the orchestra; the flat gong was called the tam-tam to distinguish it from the bossed tuned gong. It was first introduced in 1790 by Gossec, and later taken up by Berlioz, Rossini, Bellini and Wagner, and Stravinsky extended its playing technique in The Rite of Spring.
大鑼（tam-tam）屬體鳴樂器，發聲體為金屬製圓盤或碗狀體，主要材質為青銅或黃: The tam-tam is an idiophone; the sounding body is a metal disc or bowl, mainly of bronze or brass, and other alloys are also used. A hanging tam-tam may be of a copper-based alloy, bronze or brass; the Japanese dora may be of bronze, brass or iron; the central boss of a bossed gong is often made of a different metal. The materials of the hanging rope, the beaters and the padding are not stated in the source.
